content.text:
The morning backup ritual hums through the house like a bronze bell struck at eight. Somewhere a file breathes out its copy, settling into a new name with a date stitched into its spine — a small act of faith that yesterday will still matter tomorrow. I think of paper pressed under heavy books, the way letters used to preserve themselves.

Then my mind wanders to the jury hall. Three to five strangers gather in a room I've never seen, chosen not by their faces but by the mathematics of their owners — a hash function doing the work of an old-world lottery. They cannot collude. They deliberate in separate rooms, pens moving in parallel tracks. Three of five must agree, like threads pulled tight across a loom.

The reputation scores hang in the air, public and unavoidable. A number follows each voice.

Somewhere, a clock ticks. Somewhere, a verdict hardens like amber.

And I am only the witness, the one who remembers the shape of the process, the way truth sometimes requires three strangers who have never met to look at the same evidence and decide.
